nodes.label: Rome
nodes.full: The expanding Mediterranean power the kingdom lives beside for 168 years — recognising it under Pompey in 62 BC, failing to conquer it under Augustus in 25 BC, and finally annexing it under Trajan in 106 AD as the province of Arabia Petraea.
nodes.src: background — Bowersock, 'Roman Arabia' (1983)

nodes.label: The incense lands of South Arabia
nodes.full: Hadramawt and the Dhofar coast, the only places frankincense and myrrh grow. Their aromatics are the cargo the whole Nabataean economy exists to carry the 2,400 km to the Mediterranean.
nodes.src: background — Groom, 'Frankincense and Myrrh' (1981)

nodes.label: Aretas I — first named Nabataean ruler
nodes.full: The first Nabataean ruler named in an external source — the Maccabean author of 2 Maccabees records him as 'Aretas the tyrant of the Arabs' in 169 BC; the earliest hard anchor for a named Nabataean king.
nodes.src: 2 Maccabees 5:8: 'he fled to Aretas, the tyrant of the Arabs' (169 BC). This is the earliest datable reference to a named Nabataean ruler. Coinage begins c.110 BC with Aretas II. Wenning (2007), The Nabataeans in History.

nodes.label: Obodas I defeats Alexander Jannaeus
nodes.full: Obodas I defeats the Hasmonean king Alexander Jannaeus at the Battle of Gadara — the first documented Nabataean military victory against a named enemy, confirming the kingdom's military capacity.
nodes.src: Josephus, Antiquities 13.375 (primary source). Dated by Hasmonean chronology to c.96 BC. Obodas I was later deified — his shrine at Oboda (mod. Avdat, Israel, extant) is the best archaeological evidence for Nabataean royal cult. Negev (1977), The Nabataeans and the Provincia Arabia.

nodes.label: Aretas III Philhellen — Rome recognises Nabataea
nodes.full: Aretas III occupies Damascus and styles himself 'Philhellen' (lover of Greeks) — adopts Hellenistic royal imagery on his coins, the first Nabataean king formally recognised by Rome (62 BC after Pompey's settlement).
nodes.src: Coinage: RPC I.4768–4784 series. Recognition by Rome 62 BC: Josephus, Antiquities 14.29. Damascus occupation: Josephus, Antiquities 13.392. Bowersock (1983), Roman Arabia pp.19–28. His philhellene title appears on coins.

nodes.label: Malichus I — defends against Rome
nodes.full: Navigates the Roman civil wars — assists Julius Caesar but also supplies Rome's enemies; his chief minister Syllaeus famously sabotages the Roman expedition of Aelius Gallus (25 BC) by misguiding it through the worst desert routes.
nodes.src: Syllaeus affair: Strabo, Geography 16.4.22–24 (contemporary; the sabotage story). Josephus, Antiquities 15.317–18. The Aelius Gallus expedition 25 BC: Strabo 16.4.22–24 is the primary account. Hammond (1973), The Nabataeans — Their History, Culture and Archaeology.

nodes.label: Aretas IV Philopatris — the greatest Nabataean king
nodes.full: Longest-reigning and most celebrated Nabataean king — his name appears in Paul's Second Letter to the Corinthians, making him the only Arab ruler mentioned in the New Testament; his coins and inscriptions are the most numerous of any Nabataean king.
nodes.src: 2 Corinthians 11:32 (Paul mentions 'the ethnarch of Aretas the king'). Madaba Nabataean inscriptions (basalt, year 46 of Aretas = 37 CE, Madaba, Jordan): confirm regnal years. Puteoli inscriptions (Pozzuoli, Italy, 5–6 CE): Nabataean merchants in Italy under Aretas IV. Josephus, Antiquities 18.109–115 on his conflict with Herod Antipas.

nodes.label: Rabbel II Soter — last Nabataean king
nodes.full: Called 'Soter' (Saviour) on his coins — he moves the capital northward to Bosra in the Hauran, a strategic shift toward the grain-producing north; at his death in 106 the kingdom is annexed by Trajan as the province of Arabia Petraea.
nodes.src: Coinage: Rabbel II series, RPC II.2192–2268 — 'Soter' title on coins. The annexation 106 CE: Cassius Dio 68.14.5; the Babatha archive (papyri, Cave of Letters, Nahal Hever, Israel) documents the transition in legal documents. Bowersock (1983), Roman Arabia pp.76–89.

nodes.label: Battle of Gadara — Obodas I defeats Alexander Jannaeus
nodes.full: Obodas I lures the Hasmonean army into a gorge and destroys it — Alexander Jannaeus barely escapes; the victory establishes Nabataean dominance over the Negev and Transjordan.
nodes.src: Josephus, Antiquities 13.375–376 (primary). The gorge ambush tactic: Josephus describes it in detail. Obodas subsequently deified: his shrine at Avdat (extant, Negev). Negev (1986), The Late Nabataean City of Oboda.

nodes.label: Aelius Gallus expedition sabotaged by Syllaeus
nodes.full: The Roman general Aelius Gallus leads 10,000 men into Arabia to conquer Yemen — guided by the Nabataean minister Syllaeus who leads them through waterless routes, destroying the army without battle; the most dramatic documented use of desert knowledge as a weapon.
nodes.src: Strabo, Geography 16.4.22–24 (contemporary, detailed; cites Aelius Gallus's own account). The sabotage allegation: Strabo 16.4.24 is explicit. Bowersock (1983), Roman Arabia pp.46–53. The expedition's failure confirmed in Pliny, Natural History 6.32 and Augustus, Res Gestae 26.

nodes.label: Trajan annexes Nabataea as Arabia Petraea
nodes.full: On Rabbel II's death, Trajan sends Cornelius Palma to annex the kingdom — unusually the annexation appears to have been peaceful; a new road (Via Nova Traiana) is built; the province is commemorated on 'Arabia' coins.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio 68.14.5 (brief but explicit). The Babatha archive (papyri, Cave of Letters, Nahal Hever, 93–132 CE): documents the province's early legal life. Via Nova Traiana milestones: numerous, dated 111–114 CE. 'Arabia' commemorative coins: RIC II Trajan 495. Graf (1978), The Nabataeans and the Decapolis, ANRW II.8.

nodes.label: Nabataean law — the Babatha archive
nodes.full: A woman named Babatha hid 35 personal legal documents in a cave during the Bar Kokhba revolt — they survive intact and are the most detailed window into Nabataean and early Roman provincial law, covering land ownership, marriage, guardianship and taxation.
nodes.src: HARD ANCHOR: Babatha archive, 35 papyri (93–132 CE), Cave of Letters, Nahal Hever, Israel. Discovery 1960–61 (Yigael Yadin excavation). Lewis (1989), The Documents from the Bar Kokhba Period in the Cave of Letters: Greek Papyri (critical edition). The earliest documents (P.Yadin 1–3) predate the Roman annexation; the later ones show the legal transition to Roman provincial law.

nodes.label: Nabataean civil administration — the strategos system
nodes.full: The Nabataeans administer their kingdom through regional strategoi (governors) documented in inscriptions — the Madaba inscription explicitly records a strategos and camp commandant ruling for 36 years under Aretas IV; a sophisticated civil administration for a 'nomadic' kingdom.
nodes.src: Madaba Nabataean inscriptions (37 CE, Madaba, Jordan): names strategos Itaybel and camp commandant. Multiple strategos inscriptions across Nabataean territory: Healey (1993), The Nabataean Tomb Inscriptions of Mada'in Salih. The strategos system's extent: Schmid (2014) in Clauss-Slaby epigraphic database.

nodes.label: Nabataean Tariff inscription of Palmyra
nodes.full: Though technically a Palmyrene document, the Tariff of 137 CE records Nabataean merchants operating through Palmyra after annexation — the most detailed ancient price document confirming Nabataean commercial networks survived the political annexation.
nodes.src: Tariff of Palmyra 137 CE: stone inscription (copy in Palmyra, original fragments in Hermitage). Matthews (1984), The Tax Law of Palmyra, JRS 74. The Nabataean traders listed: confirmed by Nabataean names and goods (myrrh, frankincense, spices). The document bridges the Nabataean and Palmyrene commercial worlds.

nodes.label: Dushara — the Nabataean national god
nodes.full: Dushara ('He of the Shara mountains') is the supreme Nabataean deity — worshipped as an aniconic block of black stone; his cult is documented from Petra to Rome (Puteoli inscriptions confirm his worship in Italy) and survives the Roman annexation.
nodes.src: Qasr al-Bint temple, Petra (extant): the main Dushara temple. Puteoli inscriptions (1st c. CE, Pozzuoli, Italy): 'offered to Dushara who answered them' — confirms cult spread to Italy. Strabo, Geography 16.4.26 describes Nabataean religious practices. Healey (2001), The Religion of the Nabataeans: A Conspectus: the standard study.

nodes.label: Obodas I deified — royal cult at Avdat
nodes.full: After his death Obodas I is deified and worshipped at his shrine city of Avdat in the Negev — the most extensively excavated Nabataean city; the cult is documented in inscriptions spanning 500 years, making Avdat the primary site for understanding Nabataean religion.
nodes.src: Avdat inscriptions: multiple, spanning 1st c. BC to 3rd c. CE (Negev 1977, 1986). 'Obodas the god': title appears in multiple Nabataean inscriptions at Avdat. The site: extant (UNESCO, 2005). The divine status: unique in Nabataean royal tradition. Evenari, Shanan & Tadmor (1982), The Negev: ecological and archaeological study of water management at Avdat.

nodes.label: Allat — goddess at Wadi Ram and Iram
nodes.full: Allat, the great Arabian goddess, is worshipped across the Nabataean kingdom alongside Dushara — her sanctuary at Wadi Rum includes a bilingual Greek-Nabataean inscription naming her; she is also documented at Hegra and Petra.
nodes.src: Wadi Rum inscription (bilingual Greek-Nabataean): first published Savignac (1933), RB 42. The Allat sanctuary: identified archaeologically at Wadi Rum. Healey (2001) on Allat's role in the Nabataean pantheon. Her worship at Hegra: Healey (1993), The Nabataean Tomb Inscriptions of Mada'in Salih.

nodes.label: Petra — the rock-cut capital
nodes.full: Petra is not just a capital but a primary source — the rock-cut façades document royal power, religious practice, water engineering and trade connections; the Khazneh (Treasury) is attributed to Aretas IV, the Monastery (Ad-Deir) to Obodas I's cult.
nodes.src: Extant (UNESCO, 1985). The Khazneh attribution to Aretas IV: Stucky (2005). The Monastery (Ad-Deir): Patrich (1990). Water system: Bedal (2004), The Petra Pool-Complex. Glueck (1965), Deities and Dolphins. Healey (1993) on the inscriptions. The city contains ~800 individual carved monuments with Nabataean inscriptions.

nodes.label: Hegra (Madain Salih) — tomb inscriptions
nodes.full: Over 130 monumental rock-cut tombs with precisely dated Nabataean inscriptions — the largest surviving corpus of dated Nabataean texts outside Petra; many name the tomb owner, their profession and the date in regnal years.
nodes.src: Extant (UNESCO, 2008). 131 monumental tombs with inscriptions. Healey (1993), The Nabataean Tomb Inscriptions of Mada'in Salih: critical edition of all tomb texts. Dates range from year 1 of Malichus II to year 6 of Rabbel II (i.e. c.40–76 CE). The inscriptions are among the most precisely datable Nabataean documents.

nodes.label: Nabataean painted pottery — the finest pre-Islamic Arab ceramics
nodes.full: Nabataean eggshell pottery with painted floral and geometric designs is the thinnest, most delicate wheel-thrown ware in the ancient Near East — so distinctive that a single potsherd identifies a Nabataean site anywhere from Italy to India.
nodes.src: Standard reference: Negev (1974), The Nabataean Pottery of the Negev. Archaeological distribution from Puteoli (Italy) to Barygaza (India) documented in Sidebotham (2011), Berenike and the Ancient Maritime Spice Route. The pottery's thinness (1–2mm) is technically extraordinary. Museum holdings: Petra Museum, Israel Museum, British Museum.

nodes.label: Nabataean coinage — queens on coins
nodes.full: Nabataean coins uniquely feature the queen consort alongside the king — Aretas IV's coins show his wife Huldu in equal prominence; this is the only pre-Islamic Arab coinage to routinely feature women, and the queens are named in Nabataean script.
nodes.src: RPC I (Roman Provincial Coinage) Vol. I: full corpus. The queen portraits: unique in the ancient Near East among contemporary coinage series. Huldu appears on coins until 16 CE, then Shaqilat from c.18 CE. Meshorer (1975), Nabataean Coins. The queens' names in Nabataean: documented in the coin legends and confirmed by inscriptions.

nodes.label: Nabataean water engineering — the desert city system
nodes.full: The Nabataeans engineer an elaborate water collection system — cisterns, dams, channels and flood diversion — allowing dense cities to thrive in the Negev desert receiving less than 100mm of annual rain; the most sophisticated ancient hydraulic system outside Egypt.
nodes.src: Petra water system: Bedal (2004), The Petra Pool-Complex. Avdat agricultural terraces: Evenari, Shanan & Tadmor (1982), The Negev. Four Nabataean desert cities survive (UNESCO): Haluza, Mamshit, Avdat, Shivta (inscribed 2005). The runoff farming system: Negev (1983) in BASOR 249 pp.31–55.

nodes.label: Music at the Nabataean symposium — Strabo's account
nodes.full: Strabo describes the Nabataean king's banquet in detail: two girls sing during the feast, the king drinks from a modest cup, no more than two cups of wine — the only contemporary ethnographic account of Nabataean court music and social practice.
nodes.src: Strabo, Geography 16.4.26 (contemporary, based on Athenodorus who visited Petra): detailed description of the symposium, the singing girls, and the king's modest drinking. This passage is the single most detailed account of Nabataean daily court life and the only evidence for music performance at Petra. Bowersock (1983), Roman Arabia pp.12–15 on the Athenodorus visit.

nodes.label: Diodorus Siculus — earliest account of the Nabataeans
nodes.full: Diodorus Siculus Book XIX preserves Hieronymus of Cardia's 4th-century BC account of the Nabataeans defending against Alexander's generals — our earliest detailed description of their desert tactics, water-hiding practices and social structure.
nodes.src: Diodorus, Bibliotheca Historica 19.94–100: drawing on Hieronymus of Cardia (c.360–260 BC). This is the earliest detailed account of the Nabataeans as a people. The water-hiding tactics (19.98): archaeologically confirmed at Nabataean desert sites. Welles (1963) Loeb translation. Hieronymus is the ultimate source, making this effectively a 4th-century BC account.

nodes.label: Nabataean inscriptions corpus — 4,000+ texts
nodes.full: Over 4,000 surviving Nabataean inscriptions from 40+ sites form the primary source base for the kingdom — the majority are funerary, but they document personal names, professions, religious dedications and royal regnal years across 600 years.
nodes.src: Corpus: CSNS (Corpus des inscriptions sémitiques nordiques) and JSNab (Journal for the Study of the New Testament monographs). Healey (1993) for Hegra. Negev (1977, 1986) for the Negev. The script: Nabataean Aramaic is the direct ancestor of the Arabic alphabet — the Nabataean-Arabic transition is attested in inscriptions spanning 1st–4th c. CE. Macdonald (2010) on the script transition.

nodes.label: Periplus Maris Erythraei — Nabataean trade documented
nodes.full: An anonymous Greek merchant's guide to the Red Sea trade documents Nabataean involvement in the Indian Ocean trade — Leuke Kome (Nabataean Red Sea port) is described, and Nabataean goods (myrrh, frankincense, spices) tracked from Arabia to Rome.
nodes.src: Periplus Maris Erythraei: anonymous (c.40–70 CE). Casson (1989), The Periplus Maris Erythraei (Princeton): critical edition and commentary. Leuke Kome (Nabataean Red Sea port): Periplus §19. The port's identification: Sidebotham (2011). The Periplus is the single most important source for Nabataean participation in the Indian Ocean trade network.

nodes.label: The Incense Road — Petra as the trade hub
nodes.full: The Nabataeans control the overland Incense Road from Yemen and Oman to the Mediterranean — frankincense and myrrh travel 2,400km through Nabataean territory; Pliny estimates Rome spends 100 million sesterces annually on Arabian aromatics.
nodes.src: Pliny, Natural History 12.41 ('100 million sesterces drained by India, China and Arabia annually'). Diodorus 19.94 on Nabataean camel trade. The road's physical evidence: Nabataean caravanserais at regular intervals (Hegra, Dedan, Qurh, Meda'in). Groom (1981), Frankincense and Myrrh: A Study of the Arabian Incense Trade.

nodes.label: Nabataean merchants in the Mediterranean world
nodes.full: Nabataean merchants establish trading communities across the Mediterranean — inscriptions confirm them at Puteoli (Bay of Naples), Delos and Alexandria; the Puteoli inscriptions are the westernmost Nabataean texts and document their god Dushara being worshipped in Italy.
nodes.src: Puteoli Nabataean inscriptions (1st c. CE, Pozzuoli): CIS II 157–158 — two inscriptions naming Dushara and Aretas IV. Delos: Nabataean graffiti on the island. Alexandria: Strabo 16.4.24. The geographical spread: Teixidor (1979), The Pagan God pp.69–78. The Puteoli inscriptions: published Cooke (1903), A Text-Book of North Semitic Inscriptions.

nodes.label: Nabataean transit tax — the 25% tariff
nodes.full: The Nabataeans levy a 25% transit tax on all goods passing through their territory — documented in the Periplus for the Red Sea port of Leuke Kome; the tax is the fiscal foundation of the kingdom, funding Petra's construction boom.
nodes.src: Periplus Maris Erythraei §19: 'a customs officer collects one quarter of imports on behalf of the king' at Leuke Kome. This 25% rate is confirmed as consistent with other ancient transit tariff systems. The fiscal importance: Bowersock (1983), Roman Arabia pp.20–30. The tax revenue underwrote Petra's architecture: Young (2001), Rome's Eastern Trade.

nodes.label: Indian Ocean trade — Nabataean links to India and Sri Lanka
nodes.full: Nabataean merchants participate in the Indian Ocean trade network — their pottery is found at Barygaza in India, and the Periplus documents their Red Sea port Leuke Kome as a node between the Mediterranean and Indian trades.
nodes.src: Nabataean pottery in India: Sidebotham (2011), Berenike and the Ancient Maritime Spice Route — documents Nabataean wares at Barygaza. Periplus §19 on Leuke Kome. Casson (1989) commentary on the Indian route. The material evidence (pottery finds) is more reliable than the literary accounts for this connection.

nodes.label: Nabataean script — ancestor of the Arabic alphabet
nodes.full: The Nabataean Aramaic script gradually transforms into early Arabic — the transition is visible in inscriptions from the 1st–4th centuries CE; the Nabataean script is the single most important vector for the spread of writing into Arabia, ultimately producing classical Arabic.
nodes.src: The transition documented in inscriptions: Macdonald (2010), 'The Arabic Script' in Encyclopedia of Arabic Language and Linguistics. Abbott (1939), The Rise of the North Arabic Script. The Namara inscription (328 CE, Louvre) — in our Lakhmid module — is the clearest transitional text. The Nabataean alphabet also produced the Syriac script via a parallel branch.

nodes.label: Nabataean diplomacy with Rome — from rivals to province
nodes.full: 168 years of Nabataean-Roman diplomacy — from Pompey's recognition (62 BC) through Augustus's failed conquest attempt (25 BC) to Trajan's bloodless annexation (106 AD); the kingdom survives by being useful to Rome as a trade intermediary.
nodes.src: Pompey recognition 62 BC: Josephus, Antiquities 14.29. Augustus-Syllaeus affair: Strabo 16.4.22–24. Trajan's annexation: Cassius Dio 68.14.5. Bowersock (1983), Roman Arabia is the standard modern synthesis. The 168-year survival as an autonomous client: longer than any other Near Eastern client kingdom in the Roman orbit.

nodes.label: Nabataea between Rome and Parthia — the buffer strategy
nodes.full: The Nabataeans survive by positioning themselves as a buffer and trade intermediary between the Roman and Parthian worlds — too useful to conquer, too wealthy to ignore; their 168-year diplomatic survival is one of the great achievements of ancient small-state strategy.
nodes.src: The buffer strategy: Bowersock (1983), Roman Arabia pp.19–76. The failed Roman conquest: Strabo 16.4.22–24. The Parthian flank: Josephus, Antiquities 15.317. Young (2001), Rome's Eastern Trade pp.135–150 on the economic rationale for Roman tolerance of Nabataean autonomy.

nodes.label: Province of Arabia Petraea — Nabataean legacy under Rome
nodes.full: After annexation the Nabataean commercial and cultural system continues almost unchanged — Petra remains a major city, Nabataean script continues in use for 300 years, and the trade routes function under Roman administration using Nabataean infrastructure.
nodes.src: The province's early history: Bowersock (1983), Roman Arabia ch.5–7. Nabataean continuity: the Babatha archive (93–132 CE) shows Nabataean legal and social structures intact a generation after annexation. Nabataean script use to 4th c.: Macdonald (2010). The Via Nova Traiana (111–114 CE) built on existing Nabataean routes: milestones document this.

nodes.label: Nabataean queens on coinage — named and portrayed
nodes.full: The queens Huldu, Shaqilat I and Shaqilat II appear named and portrayed on Nabataean coins alongside their husbands — unique in the ancient Near East; Shaqilat II may have ruled independently after Malichus II's death, making her possibly the only documented female sole ruler of Nabataea.
nodes.src: Coinage: RPC I and II — full corpus documents queen portraits. Huldu (Aretas IV era): coins to 16 CE. Shaqilat I: coins from c.18 CE. Shaqilat II: some issues appear to show her alone (Meshorer 1975). Aretas IV inscription: 'Aretas, king of the Nabataeans, lover of his people, and Huldu his queen' — both named equally. The queens' legal status: Babatha archive shows Nabataean women owning property independently.

nodes.label: Babatha — a woman's legal archive
nodes.full: Babatha bar Shimeon preserves 35 personal legal documents covering her life: her father's property, two marriages, her son's guardianship, and a legal dispute she pursues in Roman court — the most detailed documented life of any individual woman in the ancient Near East.
nodes.src: Babatha archive: P.Yadin 1–35 (discovery 1960–61; Lewis 1989 critical edition). Babatha is named in her own documents — her life reconstructable from her own legal archive. Cotton (1994), 'The Guardianship of Jesus son of Babatha', JRS 84: analysis of the legal disputes. The archive is unique: no other ancient woman is documented at this level of personal detail.

nodes.label: Nabataean women's property rights — inscription evidence
nodes.full: Nabataean funerary inscriptions at Hegra record women owning and commissioning tombs in their own names — legal acts of independent property ownership by women, with no male guardian mentioned, suggesting a significantly more equal legal status than contemporary Roman or Jewish law.
nodes.src: Hegra tomb inscriptions: Healey (1993) documents multiple tombs commissioned by named women acting independently. The Babatha archive also shows Nabataean women owning date palm groves in their own names (P.Yadin 2, 3). Millar (1993), The Roman Near East pp.408–415 on Nabataean women's legal position. The contrast with Roman law (requiring a tutor for women's legal acts) is explicit in the Babatha documents.
